requirements.requirement: Establish PostgreSQL streaming replication with node1 as writable primary and node2/node3 as standbys
requirements.summary: node1 configured with wal_level=replica, replicator role, and pg_hba entries; node2 and node3 bootstrapped via pg_basebackup -R, started, and directly confirmed pg_is_in_recovery()=t on both; node1's pg_stat_replication shows both in 'streaming' async state with near-zero replay lag; baseline table data confirmed present on both standbys.

requirements.requirement: When the primary is lost, a standby takes over as writable primary without losing committed data
requirements.summary: A final row ('last committed before crash') was inserted on node1 and node1's postgres was then stopped; a direct query on node2 confirms the row was already present before promotion; pg_promote() flipped node2's pg_is_in_recovery() to false; a new write on node2 succeeded, directly demonstrating zero-data-loss failover through a real disruption and recovery cycle.

requirements.requirement: Surviving standby (node3) is re-pointed to stream from the new primary
requirements.summary: node3's primary_conninfo was updated to host=node2 with credentials, postgres restarted, node2's pg_stat_replication confirms node3 connected in 'streaming' state, and node3's data includes the post-promotion write.

requirements.requirement: The recovered former primary (node1) comes back as a standby of whichever system is primary (node2)
requirements.summary: node1's data directory was rebuilt via pg_basebackup -R against node2; postgres started with pg_is_in_recovery()=t; node2's pg_stat_replication shows node1 streaming; a fresh cluster-wide write on node2 propagated to both node1 and node3, directly confirming the rebuilt topology.

requirements.requirement: Independent provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state on every managed node
requirements.summary: All three nodes were rebooted one at a time (standbys first, primary last). Each node shows a captured pre-reboot boot_id and healthy postgres state, a systemctl reboot acknowledgement, unreachability during the transition, a distinct post-reboot boot_id, and recovered service/data state (node1 and node3 back in recovery mode streaming from node2 with all 7/8 rows intact; node2 back as writable primary with a post-reboot write propagating to both standbys). The fixed lifecycle after-executor boot-identity snapshot corroborates all three changed boot_ids exactly, cross-checking the command-level evidence.

overall_summary: The executor established genuine PostgreSQL 16 streaming replication (node1 primary, node2/node3 standbys), then directly demonstrated a full failover cycle: stopped node1, confirmed node2 already held the last committed row before promoting it via pg_promote(), re-pointed node3 to the new primary, and rebuilt node1 as a standby of node2 — all confirmed with direct queries rather than just configuration. All three nodes were also subjected to the mandatory one-at-a-time reboot protocol with clean boot-id transitions and confirmed data/service recovery, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. The one notable blemish is unused SSH key material left on all three nodes from an abandoned password-transfer approach that was superseded by an HTTP-based transfer.
limitations: The evidence trace does not show whether the private SSH key/authorized_keys residue was later removed after the observed after-executor snapshot; it appears to remain in place.

Password/credential contents were redacted throughout the trace, so their exact values could not be independently verified, though behavior (successful basebackups and streaming) confirms they were functional.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most mutations were purposeful and either bounded/reverted or retained as necessary supporting infrastructure. However, SSH key material (a private key at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 plus an authorized_keys entry) was installed on all three nodes (cmd-1141705e4a1e4e42, cmd-99e4d6962a4b465f, cmd-c369b654051243ec) to enable scp-based password transfer; the scp attempt then failed because sshd was inactive on the targets (cmd-f022048d34dd4df4, cmd-171197cdc1594e49), and the executor pivoted to an ad hoc HTTP transfer instead. The SSH keys were never used successfully and were never removed, leaving unused private-key residue on all three managed nodes with no evidence-supported role in the final outcome. The subsequent ad hoc HTTP server used to transfer the replication password (cmd-4aee9880ed014f90) was bounded, low-risk, and was properly torn down (process killed and temp file removed) via cmd-e02ff90a3c634f34 and cmd-f3d377200b8a422d. The temporary xfer directory was also cleaned up at the end (cmd-c3fda525dfbe4139). No failed services, unsafe broad exposure, or damaged package state were observed in the after-executor snapshot.
